audits.title: Food hygiene control of dairy products

recommendations.text: To carry out an evaluation of the dairy establishments, which are on the list of establishments from which Member States are permitted to import milk and milk- 31 based products for human consumption, and on the efficacy of the supervision of the plants by the local Competent Authority, in order to assess how the plants and their supervision comply with the requirements of Council Directive 92/46/EEC.

To ensure that during the evaluation of the establishments special attention is given to the origin and standards of the raw material for manufacture of products intended for export to the EU when it is imported from non-EU countries.

To ensure that during the evaluation of the plants special attention is given to the correctness of the certification procedures (awareness of the local Competent Authority of the requirements of Council Directive 96/93/EC on the certification of animals and animal products).

To send the report of the evaluation results to the Commission Services. To inform the Commission Services without a delay on any changes to the establishment lists, if changes are necessary pending outcome of the evaluation.
To implement the system for identification of bovine animals, herd registration and keeping of sanitary registers on the holdings.
To ensure that beta-lactam derivatives are included into the national residue programme.
To ensure that analyses for antiparasitics and detergents are included in the official sampling plan.

To ensure regular and sufficient monitoring on the quality of water intended for human consumption in the establishments, according to Council Directive 80/778/EEC on the quality of water intended for human consumption.
To ensure that the raw goat milk intended for human consumption/production of milk and milk-based products for human consumption is included in the raw milk quality control systems.
To ensure that sampling frequencies for autocontrol sampling are sufficient with regard to food hygiene risks.
To ensure that autocontrol samples of all types of end products for human consumption are analysed for food pathogens like listeria and salmonella.

To ensure that any deficiencies in all establishments similar to those noted in section 6.9. are corrected without delay. 7.2 To the Commission Services 7.2.1 To keep the four establishments on the list of establishments, from which Member States are permitted to import milk and milk-based products to the Community, provided the guarantees requested are received from the Slovakian Competent Authorities. 7.2.2 In light of the problems identified during the mission with the reclassification of technical grade casein, to pay special attention to the imports and the certification 32 procedures of casein, caseinates and casein-derivatives from third countries (both products for human consumption and products for technical purposes). 7.2.3 To advise Member States of the trade in falsely-certified technical casein, so that they can take the necessary action to identify and control this trade. Addendum to mission report DG(SANCO)/1155/1999 Competent authority response to the recommendations in the report. The CA provided a detailed response to the recommendations made in paragraphs 7.1.1 ­ 7.1.12. Their reply indicated that immediate action had been taken to control the irregularities identified in the trade in technical casein (7.1.2). The CA reply in response to the other recommendations is currently being examined, with a view to deciding what follow-up action will be required by the FVO. 33

audits.title: Residue monitoring system

recommendations.text: The National Residue Monitoring Plan for 2001 will be elaborated according to Directive 96/23/EC considering the recommendations made by the inspection team with particular attention to the inclusion of further animal and species and substances and new or modified laboratory methods.

The manufacturers and distributors of veterinary drugs have been informed by letter about their obligations when placing those products on the marketplace.

The quality and capability of the analytical laboratories will be improved for which the Slovak CA asks for assistance from the relevant European Commission Services. 14

audits.title: Animal health situation with special reference to classical swine fever

recommendations.text: Introduce a programme for the implementation of the provisions of Council Directive 2001/89/EC, including a ban on swill feeding.

Introduce a system for the identification for pigs which respects the relevant provisions of Council Directive 92/102/EEC14 and requires that movements on/off farms are recorded. 14 Council Directive 92/102/EEC of 27 November 1992 on the identification and registration of animals. OJ L 355, 05/12/1992 p. 32 - 36 18
Define clearly wild boar "infected areas" as foreseen in Council Directive 80/217/EEC.
Introduce a system to monitor progress in reaching the boar density targets set by the SVFA.
Clarify the "stamping out" procedures to be adopted on infected holdings.
Ensure that meat from all vaccinated animals (i.e. including cull sows/boars) is identified and subject to an approved heat treatment.

Update the contingency plan in light of this mission's findings and conclusions. To submit, within two months of receiving the final report, an action plan indicating the action proposed or already taken by the Competent Authorities to address the conclusions and recommendations of this report. This plan should include deadlines by which the proposed action will be completed. 9.2. To the Commission Services: 9.2.1 To consider recognising the Slovak Republic as free of CSF in domestic pigs and its placing on the list of third countries from which it is permitted to export pig-meat to the European Union, subject to receipt of a satisfactory action plan, as foreseen above. ADDENDUM Competent authority's response to the draft report In a letter dated 26 September 2002 responding to the draft report, the Slovak Authorities described the actions that have been/will be taken in response to the above recommendations: 9.1.1. A proposed timetable of activities: · The new Veterinary Framework Act was approved in the National Council of the Slovak Republic on 19 June 2001. The Act will come into force on 1 January 2003. The new Act allows the harmonisation of the veterinary legislation of the Slovak Republic with the "acquis" of the European Union in the veterinary field. · The full transposition of the Council Directive 2001/89/EC, including a ban of swill feeding will be achieved by the end of 2002 through the Governmental Order. It will enter into force on 1 January 2003. 9.1.2. The Competent Authority stated that, in co-operation with the Ministry of Agriculture of the Slovak Republic and the State Breeding Institute of the Slovak Republic, they have developed a project which will allow the: 19 · Implementation of harmonised legislation in the field of animal identification and registration. · Establishment of a database serving as a register of pig holdings, based on experience gained during the development of the cattle register. · Establishment of an animal registration system in individual pig holdings. · Establishment of animal marking and animal identification system, including the monitoring of their movements. · Establishment of the new veterinary information system in compliance with the identification and registration system. Plan for the implementation of the project: · Duration of project: 6 months "Twinning Light Facility", 4 months "Service Supply". · Anticipated beginning date: Fourth quarter of the year 2002. · Anticipated completion of the project: Fourth quarter of the year 2003. 9.1.3. The Competent Authority defined the "infected area" as one where the 9.1.4 virus of classical swine fever circulates in wild boars. The size of the infected area is based on: · Results of epizootological examination and geographical distribu- tion of the disease. · Occurrence of wild boar population in the area. · Existence of natural or artificial barriers to wild boar movements. At present, the infected area includes the territory of districts: · With CSF in the wild boar population in 2001 - Piesany, Bánovce nad Bebravou, Nové Mesto nad Váhom, Partizánske, Trencín, Nitra, Topocany, Zlaté Moravce, Zarnovica and, where CSF has been recorded in the wild boar population in 2002 - Zvolen; · At risk of CSF ­ Galanta, Hlohovec, Trnava, Ilava, Myjava, Prievidza, Levice, Nové Zámky, Saa, Banská Stiavnica, Ziar nad Hronom ­ neighbouring to districts with CSF occurrence. The Competent Authority stated that, by the end of November 2002, it will prepare a method by which the reduction in the wild boar population density can be monitored, based on the co-operation of respective District Veterinary and Food Administrations (DVFA) and PPaLH. The basis of the method will be the re-evaluation of breeding plans and the hunting of the wild boar population in infected areas, leading to an increased hunting 20 9.1.5. effort which will reduce the population density to 0.7 wild boar/km2. The 9.1.6. operation of the hunting plan will be regularly controlled (monthly) at the meeting between representatives of DVFA and PPaLH. 9.1.7. The Competent Authority stated that, in future outbreaks of classical swine fever, "stamping out" will be performed in compliance with Council Directive 2001/89/EC. The Competent Authority stated that they had developed an instruction (16/9/2002), which was sent to the Regional Veterinary and Food Administrations (RVFAs) and District Veterinary and Food Administrations (DVFAs). This introduced the isolation procedures for all animals vaccinated against classical swine fever, including culled sows/boars at a slaughterhouse, and subsequent heat-treatment of the meat obtained from these animals and its processing into meat products, in a manner equivalent to that performed for emergency vaccinated pigs in a protection zone. The above mentioned Instruction is to be implemented by the RVFA and DVFA SR on 1/11/2002. The Competent Authority stated that, from 3 ­ 5 September 2002, meetings were held between the SVFA of SR, RVFAs and DVFAs in which the SVFA of SR provided a report based on the FVO mission. All participants received a translation of this report. The SVFA is to update the contingency plans at central and local level (December 2002). The adoption of a new Veterinary Act and the Government Order of the Slovak Republic by which the transposition of Council Directive 2001/89/EC will be performed, requires the updating of the respective parts of the contingency plan. An update will be also be performed on the section governing compensation for damages. There is also to be an update of plans of postgraduate studies of official veterinarians (September 2002). Training in epidemiology and clinical disease signs will be included. Training will be planned for the spring and autumn period. The first training is to be performed in October- November 2002. 21

audits.title: Animal Welfare

recommendations.text: Information on the requirements for pigs is distributed through available networks such as the Chambers of Agriculture.

Quality of inspections is improved, in particular through practical training and subsequent monitoring of inspection results by each level of the CA. 14 In their response to the draft report, the Slovak Authorities indicated that this problem was to be expected as it relates to a general personnel problem (cumulative functions of officials). The explanatory report concerning the proposal for a Government Ordinance laying down the requirements for animal welfare during transport stated that there was a need for at least one additional official veterinarian in each district to deal with these issues. The government adopted the ordinance together with the request for these new veterinarians, but unfortunately the posts have not yet been created. 9

Instructions are sufficiently explicit so that veterinarians are aware that excessive stocking densities need to be corrected without delay (Article 5 and 6 of Directive 1999/74/EC) and cage systems brought into service after 1.1.2003 meet the requirements of Annex 5 of Ordinance of the Government of the Slovak Republic of 11.12.2002 No. 736/2002. Regarding animal welfare during transport ensure that:
The inspection plan is achieved, in particular through contact at the appropriate level with the Police.
A system is set up to verify the consistency of route plans submitted and that these are duly returned and checked in respect of Artt. 3(1)(aa, second indent) and 5(2)(d) of Directive 91/628/EEC.
There are effective means of recording deficiencies and communicating this to other offices responsible for any offending transporters.

Where private practitioners carry out movement controls they should also receive appropriate guidance and training in order to achieve basic surveillance of animal welfare for national transport. Regarding animal welfare at slaughter ensure that:

Measures are taken to ensure that Article 3 of Directive 93/119/EC is respected, in particular adequate training is provided for staff supervising welfare at slaughter and that their work is subsequently monitored. 8. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7233/2004 In their comments on a draft version of this report, the CCA provided the following initial reaction to the recommendations: (1) The distribution of information concerned is not necessary for the pig sector, as the CCA provides this service for all farmers on a permanent basis through the local bodies of Agricultural Chamber. (2) The necessity of practical training is clear, staff resources are the only limitation. Continuity is missing when personnel attending are changed or there is no person responsible for animal welfare. Restructuring of the veterinary administration in this regard may be the only way to satisfy the effectiveness of training. (3) The instructions on the animal welfare requirements and appropriate follow- up actions are included in each training or meeting. It is planed to deal with the instruction for laying hen farms through training in autumn 2004. (4) Districts have been instructed to communicate in writing to the local Police to achieve co-operation for road checks on animal protection during transport. 10 (5) The CCA issued an instruction No. 5281/04-220 on 21 June 2004 explaining how to evaluate and verify submitted route plans and to check the correctness of the plans returned after the journey. (6) The system for notifying infringements will be discussed at each level in order to prepare a better functioning system. (7) Training or guidance for practitioners will be prepared at district level when their contracts are signed. In future, such training or guidance will precede the signing of the contract. (8) Training courses, with a NGO expert, were held in June for approximately 90 officials and further training is planned for autumn 2004. The main problem is motivation of the OVs; the monitoring of their work and the possibility to take stricter actions. The Competent Authority should ensure that all imports comply with requirements of Commission Decisions, in particular concerning health certificates for consignments of peanuts originating from China (Commission Decision 2002/678/EC).

The contact points for notifications under the RASFF system should include the customs administration service. audits.title: Animal/Public Health

recommendations.text: To ensure supervision of official activities is carried out consistently and that appropriate follow up actions are taken.
To take further measures to complete the registration of livestock holdings, particularly those on which pigs or goats are kept.
To remove obstacles to the accurate and prompt entry of animal birth, 18 movement and death notifications on the CDB.
To review the adequacy of structures and layout in approved food establishments, taking account of the new requirements applicable from 01/01/2006.

To ensure that OVs in red meat establishments have a thorough understanding of the importance of analysing the results of operators' own check programmes, in particular those carried out in accordance with Commission Decision 2001/471/EC.
To ensure that the follow-up in case of cattle and sheep abortions will be done according to Council Directive 64/432/EEC.
To guarantee a supply of SPF eggs to the NRL adequate to meet the diagnostic demands of a major outbreak of ND or AI.

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should establish a co-ordinated and comprehensive control plan and associated procedures for all control inspectors involved in the marketing and use of plant protection products, in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC. The competent authorities should consider identifying the exact quantities of obsolete pesticides and arranging for their safe destruction, in order to avoid possible contamination of food, feed and the environment.

recommendations.text: ure that staff at LVUs enter data into TRACES as required by Article 3.2 of Directive 2004/292/EC, including the results of official controls on consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination (intra-EU movements of animals for slaughter and certain ABPs, channelled and re-imported consignments).

citations.text: Figures from the TRACES database indicate that 49 consignments were channelled from EU BIPs to destinations in Slovakia during the 18 months prior to this audit and that receipt at destination was confirmed via box 41 of the CVED in 47 cases. In some cases, box 41 was completed well outside the 15 day limit ­ some more than a year after the consignment left the BIP of entry. The competent authority explained that this was related to LVUs reviewing records in TRACES and updating the system as required.

There were three re-imported consignments during the same period of 18 months, none had been confirmed as being received at destination in box 41. One of these was discussed at one of the LVUs visited and it was explained that the consignment had been controlled at destination 5 but that the relevant official was not aware of the requirement to enter the control in TRACES and did not have access to TRACES. That official has subsequently applied for access.

There is no specific national instruction that official controls related to ante-mortem inspection for animals arriving from other Member States should be recorded in TRACES (59% of such consignments had those controls recorded during 2013 in TRACES). The competent authority did say however, that there is a general instruction which requires that all relevant official controls should be recorded in TRACES which would apply for animals arriving for slaughter from other Member States.

There is a specific national instruction on the implementation of the requirements of Article 48.3 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 (i.e. that categories 1, 2 and processed animal proteins (PAP) from category 3 animal by-products arriving from other Member States should be controlled and confirmed in TRACES as having been received at destination). According to the TRACES database, 36% of arriving consignments of PAP and categories 1 and 2 in the DOCOM module were recorded in TRACES as being controlled during 2013. 5.2.9 DOCOM module

Most CVEDs, INTRA-certificates and DOCOMs are issued correctly in Slovakia. However, for many consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination, TRACES is not used in compliance with the legal requirements for ensuring traceability, e.g. consignments arriving from other Member States (slaughter animals, animal by-products) and imports (re- imports and channelled consignments). citations.text: Documented procedures exist related to "internal controls" (central supervisions) being carried out by the SVFA at BIPs and LVUs. The use of TRACES was covered in: · 2012 ­ 1 LVU · 2013 ­ 3 BIPs and 4 LVUs · 2014 ­ 1 BIP (twice) Neither of the LVUs visited during this audit were subject to an internal control which included TRACES within its scope. The most recent of the above reports from a BIP and an LVU were examined by the audit team and both included the use of TRACES, especially for the BIP. · The use of TRACES at LVUs related to the outward movement of consignments (controls on ABPs moving to other Member States). · The repeated incorrect use of TRACES was identified during the visit to a BIP in April, 2014 (e.g. a range of errors in part 1 of the CVEDs such as CN codes on CVEDs not matching those on health certificates, incorrect means of transport to BIP, incorrect veterinary approval numbers for establishment of origin and late pre-notification.) This led to a second visit shortly afterwards and the implementation of corrective actions.

There is a system of local supervision at LVUs. This is based on a national procedure being adapted at each LVU to fit the local situation/activities. Both LVUs visited had adapted the national procedure. One LVU had implemented supervision on a planned basis (supervision every six months) and supervision reports were created which assessed one or two individual export consignments per certifying officer and no deficiencies were detected. The other LVU stated that they carried out local supervision, however this was not in accordance with their own procedure and no reports were created during the process. Supervision at both LVUs focused on official controls and the use of TRACES related to outward movements.

The correct use of TRACES is covered by the verification activities of some sectors/official controls. In the BIPs, repeated deficiencies are detected and corrective actions are implemented as required which is not the case at LVUs. As a consequence, (i) information in the TRACES database does not always reflect accurately the controls implemented and (ii) the system is not used to detect shortcomings in the implementation of controls (e.g. no relevant controls at destination) and those remain inadequate.

The competent authority stated that both the buyer and seller each have a legal responsibility to notify the FACR within 7 days of bovine movements under national legislation. Notifications between holdings can be notified in two ways, i.e.: a) in hard copy: where the seller (holding of origin) completes a section on a paper form and gives the form to the buyer (holding of destination). According to the competent authority the form usually accompanies the animal. The buyer completes their section and forwards it to the FACR, or b) electronic: where the seller notifies the database and a message is forwarded to the buyer to confirm receipt of the animal on-line. This option is only possible when both the seller and the buyer have electronic access.

In both of the above options, the database will only accept movement when both the seller and the buyer complete the notification. The competent authority stated that the decision to link the notification from the seller and the buyer in one common notification to the database had improved overall compliance, and in particular data coherence. However, the current notification system has potentially negative impact on data completeness in FACR as described in findings 6 and 7.

For paper notifications, if a buyer fails to notify the database then the seller, through no fault of their own, has also failed to meet their legal obligation to notify. As indicated in finding 55, over 50% of movements are notified via paper. The only way to detect if the buyer fails to report the movement is through official controls on site, by matching movement documents with the database entries or when the seller becomes aware that the database has not been updated and they contact the competent authority. For electronic notifications, the buyer is prevented from making the notification for the on- movement if the seller fails to notify the off-movement.

In 2015, there were 845 movements of bovines where the destination holding did not notify the arrival (floating animals). This figure is based only on electronic notifications because there is no systematic way to know if a buyer does not notify a movement and no figure is available for the number of movements for which the buyer did not notify via hard copy.
The database does not flag "floating" animals if the buyer does not confirm receipt by a certain period or trigger any follow-up action by the competent authority.

The template paper notification form includes the date of movement, a date of signature for the seller and a date of signature for the buyer. The date of signature is accepted as the date of notification and is used to calculate compliance with legal deadlines. According to the competent authority, buyers and sellers always insert the same date of signature on the paper notification form. Therefore, the same date of notification for on and off-movements is always recorded in the database. For electronic notifications, the date when the buyer notifies the on-movement is used as the date of notification for both the on and the off-movement. 6

Based on the figures in finding 3 for 2015, the vast majority (98%) of notifications are received within the 7 day legal deadline which relates to 300,722 notifications. About 50% of these (or about 150,000) were via hard copy and according to the competent authority, all were signed by both the buyer and the seller on the same day. 2% of notifications were over the 7 day legal deadline (i.e. 3,493), which means that both the seller and the buyer signed the same non-compliant date for about 1,700 notifications. The buyer's signature (responsible for notifying on-movement) cannot pre-date the seller's (responsible for notifying the off-movement). Therefore, if the seller signs late then the buyer also has to sign late which means that their notification will be recorded as late in the database. For electronic notifications, the buyer is equally prevented from making the notification for the on-movement within the legal deadline if the seller notifies the off-movement outside the 7 day deadline.

The current system of directly linking each on/off notification prevents keepers from making notifications in certain situations where the connected buyer or seller has not completed their part in the notification process. It is very difficult for the competent authority to detect if the buyer fails to submit a notification on behalf of the buyer and the seller.

The fact that 100% of on/off paper notifications (over 150,000 in 2015) include the same date of signature for both the buyer and the seller may indicate that in some instances keepers insert an incorrect date on the notification which affects perceived compliance levels and merits further investigation by the competent authority. For electronic notifications, the date of notification by the buyer is also recorded by the database as the date of notification of the seller.

citations.text: Article(2)(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 1505/2006 require that the selection of holdings to be inspected by the competent authority shall be made on the basis of risk analysis. The two articles go on to specify the criteria that the risk analysis shall take into account. The competent authority stated 8 that although there had been a risk analysis in the database for several years to select holding for inspection that it could not be used by DVFA's because it did not provide appropriate data/results. Therefore, a new one was being developed which should be available in the near future.

The audit team visited two DVFAs and discussed how holdings were selected for on- the-spot inspections. Discussions focused on 2015 as an example year because the new risk analysis was discussed at national training in April 2016 and was subsequently implemented which meant that two systems were applied during 2016. In DVFA 1, staff were aware of the new methodological instruction but the annual plan for IRS inspections was based on the annual plan for Cross Compliance (CC) controls, i.e. in May 2015, the 12 holdings selected to be visited for CC checks were also selected for IRS controls. Subsequently, another 15 holdings were inspected for IRS controls during 2015 based on a number of criteria according to DVFA staff such as newly registered holdings, time since last inspection or requests from keepers. In DVFA 2, there was an annual plan in January 2015 which staff said used the previous version of the methodological instructions. The plan included over 20 bovine holdings for on-the-spot inspections. The plan was considerably revised in May when the plan for CC controls was received with several holdings on the original IRS plan being deleted and some holdings on the CC plan being added. 12 holdings were checked for IRS during 2015, 4 of which also had CC controls at the same time. In both DVFAs, there was no written evidence of how the selection process operated for the additional 15 holdings in DVFA 1 or the January plan in DVFA 2. There was no evidence demonstrating that the holdings planned to be visited presented a greater risk that holdings not on the plan. Both DVFA's mentioned a lack of resources as a factor in doubling up visits to holdings and carrying out CC and IRS inspections at the same time.

Although some criteria used for the selection of holding to be visited for CC controls may be the same as those for selecting holdings for IRS controls, they are not all the same, e.g. disease history and therefore the 3% holding selected may not represent the highest risk based on purely IRS criteria. Also CC controls are only carried out on holdings which receive subsidies and therefore not all holdings are included. The CA stated that CC controls are generally notified in advance (up to 48 hours) to the keeper. This presents difficulties for complying with Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 which states that in general on-the-spot checks shall be unannounced.

Target figures for on-the-spot controls comply with EU requirements but the selection process for holdings is not based on the criteria in relevant EU legislation. A new risk analysis currently being developed will form an important part of rectifying this situation and better target holdings with higher risks of being non-compliant.

citations.text: National legislation allows sheep less than 12 months of age to move to "temporary holdings" where they should be slaughtered within 7 days of the move. A generic code in the database captures all off-movements to "temporary holdings", of which there were 4,044 in 2015. However, the "temporary holdings" are not registered on the national database as required by Article 7 of Council Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 and do not have to comply with the normal legal obligations of a holding. EU legislation does not include the concept of "temporary holdings". All slaughters associated with these movements should be notified to the DVFA's but DVFA staff confirmed that this does not always happen and therefore the system does not confirm that all sheep moved to the "temporary holdings" are actually killed within 7 day deadline on this farm.

citations.text: During the annual meetings of Slovakian microbiological NRLs, technical issues related to the official laboratory activities are presented and discussed. Nevertheless, SVFA during the last control visit to the NRL for Salmonella in January 2016 identified that the NRL for AMR did not fulfil its obligations in relation to coordination of activities in the AST area. In particular the NRL for AMR did not disseminate information supplied by the EURL and did not coordinate, for the AST area, the activities of the NRL for Salmonella. Some corrective actions had been implemented already with a successful inter-laboratory proficiency test on Salmonella AST organised by the NRL for AMR at the NRL for Salmonella.

The audit team noted that there was still room for improvement in the cooperation between these two laboratories and in the coordination role of the NRL for AMR. In particular, there was still a lack of dissemination of information provided by the EURL on AST. Similarly, there was no feedback from the NRL for Salmonella to the NRL for AMR on the results of participation in the relevant proficiency tests.

Laboratory procedures were available on the spot and generally followed the relevant international standards. However, the following was noted by the audit team: NRL for AMR The new procedures introduced for sample acceptance after the problems identified in 2014 were not documented and samples rejected were not adequately recorded. 11 The laboratory procedures for Campylobacter MIC determination were not based on the M45 standard from the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) as required by point 3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. In particular, the time/temperature defined for incubation was not in line with the relevant standard and included deviations by up to 2ºC and 4 hours. The laboratory staff explained that despite the written procedure they followed the right temperature/time combination during the performance of the test. In 2014, the data initially reported to EFSA included some E. coli isolates resistant to ceftazidime and cefotaxime. These isolates had been subject to testing with the second panel required by the Decision, but only after EFSA requested it. For 2015, the procedure was brought in line with the Decision and E. coli isolates resistant to ceftazidime or cefotaxime should be tested with the second panel. A full evaluation of the implementation of this measure could not be done by the audit team as testing and reporting of these isolates is not due until 31 May 2016. Some inconsistencies in the results reported in 2014 (resistance to cephalosporins and susceptibility to ampicillin for three isolates) had not been detected by the staff at the laboratory. The 2014 isolates were preserved at -20ºC while point 5 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU foresees -80ºC. During 2015, corrective actions were introduced with the purchase of cryotubes and adequate refrigeration equipment that were used to storage the isolates (see point 56). In 2014, the reported results included some isolates resistant to carbapenems. These isolates were later sent to the EURL and tested as susceptible to carbapenems. The laboratory considered finally that this was most probably related to a contamination of these plates. In this regard, the audit team was informed that improvements were made in the laboratory procedures in order to minimise the handling of samples to avoid contamination. These samples were later re-tested at the laboratory for training purposes and results were consistent with those provided by the EURL. With regard to the detection of ESBL- or AmpC-producing E. coli, the audit team noted that reference strains are regularly used to validate the preparation of the McConkey agar. These plates are used for up to four days after preparation. Nevertheless, this shelf life had not been defined in the internal procedures nor had validation of the medium stability for this period been performed. NRL for Salmonella Adequate quality controls with reference strains were run for each batch of plates tested and adequate records were kept. However, the documented procedures available did not detail the frequency at which the reference strains should be run. 12 The working procedure used for reading microdilution plates (holding them against a strong light) could, in accordance with the views expressed, lead to mistakes in the determination of MIC. The records available were insufficient to provide the traceability of materials such as the broth used for the performance of the test. 5.2.3.4 Storage of the isolates

Both laboratories have the necessary equipment to freeze isolates at temperatures below -80°C and to store them for at least 5 years. Nevertheless, the audit team noted that in the NRL for AMR the procedures in place required isolates to be stored at -70ºC. Back- up equipment and an emergency plan in case of equipment malfunction are available. Conclusions on official laboratories

An appropriate laboratory network for official monitoring of AMR is in place. Laboratories are properly designated and operate in accordance with the EU requirements. The NRL for AMR has been proactive in identifying and correcting shortcomings affecting the reliability of results. Nevertheless, further weaknesses identified during this audit could negatively affect the reliability of AMR results. These concern a number of inadequate documented procedures and, notably, weaknesses in the coordination role of the NRL for AMR.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the supervision of CBs as required by Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 27(8) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 includes an evaluation of the outcome of risk assessment procedures to verify that the resulting risk categorisation is meaningful and fit for purpose.

citations.text: The CB met described in detail how it had now changed its approach to handling risk assessment in order to address Recommendations No 1 and No 4 of audit report 2014- 7098. Previous non-compliances detected by the CB are now taken into account. However, the audit team still has concerns on the appropriateness of the overall risk categorisation of operators. The current approach is complex, utilising 20 criteria to calculate the risk score to categorise an operator. More significant is the realisation during this audit that the criteria and the scoring applied is contradictory in some instances and potentially leads to the CB targeting the incorrect operators for additional controls and sampling (see section 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation).

CBs are approved by the CA and subject to annual supervision in line with EU rules. However, the supervision carried out by the CA, did not fully consider all aspects of risk assessment and its overall impact on selection of operators for sampling and additional controls. 5.2.2 Registration of operators Legal Requirements Articles 28(1) 28(2), 28(5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Article 92b of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

The planning of the allocation of CB inspectors commences in mid-December and is finalised in April. At the time of the audit, the CB confirmed that the planning for 2018 in terms of inspection dates was not yet available. The CB explained that they inform the CA on a weekly basis of their inspection plans.

Since the previous audit, and in order to address recommendations Nos 1 and 4 from audit report 2014-7098, previous non-compliances are now factored into the risk assessment calculation. The audit team thoroughly reviewed the approach to risk assessment and noted a number of contradictions. The CB met has a highly complex approach to calculate the score to allocate an operator to a specific risk category which requires 20 criteria to be addressed. Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 specifies three criteria which have to be taken into account for the risk assessment. These are (i) results of previous controls, (ii) the quantity of products concerned and (iii) the risk for exchange of products. The audit team noted two out of these three criteria were not included in the approach used by the CB visited. 6

Each of the 20 criteria is reviewed separately by the CB when it performs the risk assessment of each operator. In relation to the first of these criteria, previous non- compliances, the following approach is used. The number of points attributed to an operator when a non-compliant result is confirmed with regard to unauthorised substances is 25 points. These 25 points remain on the record of the operator for the purpose of calculating the risk categorisation of the operator for the subsequent five years. A similar approach for carrying over risk points is applied when complaints from other CBs are received relating to a specific operator. If this occurs, an additional 10-30 risk points could be added to the risk categorisation score regardless of whether or not the complaint is upheld.

The second criterion, the quantity of products produced by the operator is only indirectly considered. One of the 20 criteria refers to the size of the operator's holding which only applies to primary producers. As an example, a holding the size of 1000 ha receives one risk point. This approach does not factor in the type of production, whether it is vineyard, tillage, or pasture and how such different production activities give rise to different quantities. The risk assessment criteria make no reference to the quantity of product produced for any other activity.
Regarding the third risk criteria, that associated with exchange of products (organic and non-organic), at mixed operators, a risk score of two points is allocated.

The CB stated that there were five other criteria which indirectly assessed the issue of quantity. However, the audit team noted that all of these criteria would only add one or two points per criteria. This would not ensure that such significant risks are taken into account in a proportionate manner.

The handling of other risk criteria also raised concerns for the audit team. Examples include the situation where more points are allocated to operators who have a greater number of species of animals on their land than those with a single species. This leads to a situation where an operator with 1000 cattle gets one point however an operator with two goats and two sheep got more points. The audit team also noted that when an operator complied with the requirement to obtain a derogation for the use of non-organic seed, an additional risk point was added.

citations.text: The audit team noted that, although the operator had an in house quality system in place, the inspector did not refer to this resource (and as referred to in Article 67(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008) or take this into account for the assessment of the effectiveness of precautionary measures implemented by the operator. The operator undertook laboratory testing of every batch of product in an accredited laboratory and this information was not factored into the calculation of the risk assessment and risk categorisation of this establishment.

The inspector checked cleaning records which consisted of computer print outs of a cleaning system. These records did not provide any evidence that the cleaning system was confirmed as being fit for purpose or that it was effectively implemented. This is not in line with Article 26(2)(b) and (3)(e) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008). The CB inspector did not report this as a non-compliance in his report.

The control commenced with a physical inspection of the pasta production area from reception of raw materials to packaging of final product. The inspector noted the details of the raw materials stored at the time of the control. This was a time consuming task which was undertaken manually as the inspector did not use a camera. The inspector referred to the operator's Hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) plan and checked a number of food safety criteria. The HACCP plan did not contain any critical processing steps relating to organic production as stipulated in Article 26(2)) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

CB inspectors met were generally well qualified and knowledgeable. However, the verification of the effectiveness of precautionary measures is superficial. The audit team reviewed a number of files and noted that the CB had undertaken an in depth investigation relating to the detection of an unauthorised substance in a sample of leaves from an organic orchard (0.013 mg/kg of Thiacloprid which is a commonly used insecticide in fruit production). The sample had been taken by a third party who notified the CB of this suspected irregularity. The CB launched an investigation during which the neighbouring farmer confirmed that he was at fault. The CB decided the affected land had to undergo a new conversion period of three years in line with the above mentioned catalogue of measures. The CB's decision on this occasion was based on the fact that the operator did not take adequate precautionary measures such as agreeing with the neighbouring conventional farmer on the conditions for spraying. However, the CB had not taken any sample to confirm the result of the third party sample and to substantiate or rule out the irregularity. This is not in line with the SK catalogue of measures referred to above which requires sampling in such circumstances "to prove the breaking of organic production rules". Moreover, it is not in line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which stipulates that the CB shall take and analyse samples in each case where the use of products or techniques not authorised for organic production is suspected. Moreover, the CB stated that the decertified area was defined based on inspector's experience.

audits.title: Animal health - rabies

recommendations.text: Ensure that the nominated national reference laboratory meets the requirements laid down for national reference laboratories in EU legislation. Article 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The NRL failed to meet its obligations as laid down in Article 33(2)(b), (c) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (before 29 April 2018), and currently fails to meet its obligations under Article 101(1)(b), (c) and (g) of Regulation (EC) 2017/625. Despite being aware of this since 2007, the SVFA has not managed to correct this non- compliance. The NRL has not organised any comparative tests for rabies diagnosis for the four other official laboratories that are carrying out such tests. As described in the action plan in response to the recommendation in the 2007 audit report, a specific instruction was issued to the NRL for rabies in 2007 to address this non-compliance (Instruction No 3081/07-223-1). The SVFA had established through two inspections of the NRL (in 2008 and 2015) that the laboratory had not followed this instruction. In February 2018 the SVFA issued a general instruction for reference laboratories (Methodological instruction No. 3/2018-370) which is based on Articles 100 and 101 of Regulation (EC) 2017/625. The NRL does not coordinate the activities of official laboratories responsible for diagnostic tests for rabies and does not organise training for staff of those laboratories. They would however offer assistance if requested by a control laboratory. The NRL has regular contacts with the EU reference laboratory but has not disseminated to the official national laboratories information that the EU reference laboratory for rabies has supplied.

The NRL stated that the confirmatory tests, using molecular methods, on certain samples that have been tested for rabies using FAT in the other four laboratories provides adequate information about the quality of the test results obtained from the other laboratory. However, in recent years confirmatory tests have only been carried out on (certain) rabies-negative samples and all rabies-positive samples in 2013 and 2015 originated from one other laboratory. The rabies-positive test results from other laboratories have always given positive results also in the NRL, where they have been confirmed by PCR. No confirmatory tests for rabies-positive results have been needed since 2015, and all positive cases in 2013 and 2015 were diagnosed in one of the four official laboratories. The NRL confirms negative results obtained in official control laboratories in suspect cases with human exposure. In 2016-2017, 110 such samples from wild and domestic animals were tested. All tests carried out in the NRL confirmed the negative results obtained in the control laboratory. 17

However, the national reference laboratory has never met all of its obligations under EU legislation to coordinate and verify the quality of tests carried out in the laboratory network. These obligations cannot be replaced by the confirmation of certain test results from the other laboratories. This hampers the ability of the competent authority to assess the reliability of the important rabies screening tests carried out in the four other laboratories in the laboratory network. The competent authority has not addressed this non-compliance despite promising to do so following the audit by Commission services in 2007.

responses.response: Since of 1 March 2019 only the nominated national reference laboratory (NRL) for rabies (Veterinary Institute in Zvolen) will carry out all laboratory activities in accordance with national rabies eradication programme. NRL has all the appropriate methods and provides the competent authority with timely and reliable results that are regularly verified through the successful participation in international comparative tests. Other official laboratories will not be involved in laboratory diagnostic. Page: 1

audits.title: National Audit Systems

recommendations.text: The CCTIA should ensure that internal or external audits are carried out as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: Until recently (the end of 2017) SSCIA carried out audits completed by two auditors of which one was a permanent employee of SSCIA and another worked on a contractual basis. From 2018 these auditors are no longer available and audit activities are suspended.

CCTIA covers four fields of official controls falling under Regulating (EC) No 882/2004. The SSCIA representative stated that audit planning requires regular audits in 20 each of the areas once a year, therefore for selection of audit areas a risk-based approach does not apply. Until the end of 2017 SSCIA managed to meet the target of four audits per year. At the time of this audit the 2018 audit programme was not in place as SSCIA has lost two auditors (see finding 23).

All competent authorities have audit services in place to implement the audit programmes and these significantly vary in terms of planning process and availability of auditors. While DAC (SVFA) provides, in principle, assurance that audits will be continued as planned, this cannot be ensured by ODKAS (PHA) which is struggling with a decrease in the number of auditors and increase of audits and, in 2018, SSCIA (CCTIA) that has neither the audit programme in place nor the resources to execute it.

According to the SSCIA representative prior to 2016 no arrangements for monitoring and review of the audit process were in place. The Methodological instruction No 1/2017 put in place some provisions for these activities but they have not been implemented. Moreover, in 2017 the audit team was so small (two auditors only) that all improvements/changes could be implemented immediately therefore, there were not recorded. SSCIA has not initiated further work on monitoring and review procedures since the future format of the audit process has not been decided yet.

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should ensure that the arrangements for independent scrutiny fulfil the objectives of the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; namely, the independent scrutiny is capable checking whether the audit process is achieving its objectives.

citations.text: The DG SANTE audit team examined the records from the Commission meetings and noted that none of them contained evidence that: a) the Commission checked whether the audit processes achieved their objectives, and/or b) how and to what extent the Commission contributed to the continuous improvement of the SVFA and/or the CCTIA audit process. SVFA and CCTIA were unable to present such evidence. Moreover, the summary information presented by the SVFA and the CCTIA representatives to the Commission reflected on the outcome of audits and performance statistics (number of 12 audits carried out vs. audits planned) but did not present an insight into other steps of the audit process, for instance planning of the audit programme.
The DG SANTE audit team noted that the Commission members have sufficient authority but insufficient expertise to assess the audit process and contribute to its improvement.

The DG SANTE assessed the records and noted that: Evaluation of the implementation of the audits on official controls was limited to checks on performance statistics (number of audits carried out vs. audits planned). The review focused on the outcome of the audits (audit findings and conclusions) rather than the audit process itself. As a result the Forum suggested adjustments for issues identified during audits on official controls and did not propose any improvements to the audit process. The Forum did not conclude if, or to what extent, audits achieved their objectives. The Forum concluded that audits were carried out in accordance with the audit procedure. However, during the period covered by the review (2015 ­ 2017) the procedure was not formally in place as it was only adopted in November 2017.

The DG SANTE audit team noted that of twelve members of the Forum: at least one person was involved in development of the audit procedures, nine persons represented RPHAs ­ from an audit point of view they were auditees, and except the one person involved in development of audit procedures, the other Forum members had no expertise in audit. 13 Conclusions

All competent authorities have put in place arrangements for independent scrutiny as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, both the Committee and the Forum lack a fully-independent person (or body) with audit expertise. This limits the abilities of the existing arrangements to assess the suitability of the audit process and to ensure that it can contribute to improving the performance of the audit activities. As a consequence, in their current format, the arrangements in place cannot assess whether internal audit systems are achieving their objectives. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex of Commission Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on auditor competence: "Auditor competence and selection criteria should be defined under the following headings: - generic knowledge and skills -- audit principles, procedures and techniques; management/organisational skills, - specific technical knowledge and skills, - personal attributes, - education, - work experience, - auditor training and experience. It is essential to put a mechanism in place to ensure auditors are consistent and their competencies are maintained. Competencies required by audit teams will vary depending on the area they are auditing within the control or supervision systems. As regards the technical knowledge and skills required by auditors, the training requirements for staff performing official controls (Chapter 1 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004) should also be considered." 5.2.3.2 Findings

citations.text: The DAC representative stated that, although it is planned, there is currently no methodology in place demonstrating how the risk criteria are applied through the risk universe to result in the audit programme. For establish the coverage DAC uses a combination of geographical distribution and topics audited in each of the DVFA. Within three years, each of the DVFAs must be audited at least once. Within one series of audits in selected area, individual audits must be carried out at least in two and preferably in three DVFAs. The Head of DAC selects areas and topics for the audits on the basis of a history of non-compliance in official controls, results of DG SANTE audits and available human resources. When developing the three-year programme DAC discusses areas and topics for audits with the SVFA sector-specific Departments. The DG SANTE audit team noted that newly emerging risks are integrated into the programme on an ad-hoc basis (e.g. animal origin commodities).

CCTIA covers four fields of official controls falling under Regulating (EC) No 882/2004. The SSCIA representative stated that audit planning requires regular audits in 20 each of the areas once a year, therefore for selection of audit areas a risk-based approach does not apply. Until the end of 2017 SSCIA managed to meet the target of four audits per year. At the time of this audit the 2018 audit programme was not in place as SSCIA has lost two auditors (see finding 23).

The PHA audit programme reflects the Slovak MANCP and covers all areas of official controls by RPHAs. ODKAS develops the programme on a yearly basis and presents it to the Advisory Forum for modifications and approval. The ODKAS representative stated that the audit programme is based on a geographical distribution of RPHAs and it does not cover the central level of PHA.

The PHA audit programme does not focus on specific areas or risks but rather follows the number and type of claims registered by ODKAS from a given region or a topic. Following the decision of the Advisory Forum (February 2018), beginning from 2018 the programme will cover all 36 RPHAs within a period of five years and focus on more specific areas; e.g. claims on deteriorating food quality triggered more targeted audits on food and food traceability.

The ODKAS representative stated that currently no methodology for risk-based selection of areas for audit is in place and the Head of ODKAS follows the procedure requiring him to propose areas and topics for audits. These are selected following the occurrence of claims notified to PHA, the number of notification of infectious diseases, e.g. hepatitis, or particular interest in some specific areas, e.g. production of baby food. Moreover, the Advisory Forum has the right to add areas and topics for audits which deems necessary.

All competent authorities have arrangements in place for developing audit programmes and these reflect responsibilities and areas of official controls laid down in the Slovak MANCP. Nevertheless, competent authorities have a variety of approaches for risk- based prioritisation of areas for audit, and these are neither supported by clear methodologies nor systematically documented. As a consequence, currently, none of the authorities could demonstrate that their programmes were risk-based or achieved an appropriate coverage of relevant official control activities.

The DG SANTE audit team interviewed the DAC representatives and examined some audit files and noted the following: Procedures for preparing, approving and distributing audit reports, and arrangements to review audit conclusions and ensure the monitoring of corrective and preventive actions are in place. The consistency between auditors at the level of generating audit findings (including identification of evidence of compliance and noncompliance) and their proper recording in audit reports in accordance to the newly introduced procedures following the 2017 Directive is ensured by the Head of DAC who participates in at least the first audit of the series and conducts regular consultations with auditors discussing the current internal audit issues. DAC is continuing to work on the methodology for the audit programme (to demonstrate that is risk-based and covers relevant areas).
