recommendations.text: To ensure that the methodological guidance (instructions) include the requirement that, in all circumstances, only the carcases and offal of animals that have undergone both ante- and post-mortem inspection can be declared fit for human consumption, as required by Article 45(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Operational staff must also be made aware of this requireme

citations.text: However, one of the sections of the instruction entitled "Guidelines for Veterinary Inspectors-Fresh Meat of Domestic Ungulates- Part 1, Ante-Mortem Inspection" describes the following: "Where the official veterinarian is not present at the slaughterhouse on receipt of an animal which has suffered an injury and suffers from pain or an animal which is excessively exhausted after transport and, therefore, delaying slaughter by carrying out ante-mortem inspection could cause further unnecessary suffering, the slaughterhouse operator may in exceptional cases slaughter/kill it without delay without ante mortem inspection, but must immediately inform the official veterinarian and submit to him the body and all parts necessary for the inspection.

This instruction is in contravention of Article 45(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 and in contradiction with another SVFA guidance "Guidelines for Veterinary Inspectors-Fresh Meat of Domestic Ungulates- Part 3, Post-Mortem Inspection" which, in the section on decisions concerning meat, clearly states as the first reason for considering meat as unfit for human consumption when it `comes from animals which have not undergone ante- mortem inspection'.

The SVFA issues instructions in the form of guidelines to OVs and other staff. One of such guidelines allows, in some cases and on welfare grounds, the use of meat for 16 human consumption from animals slaughtered in the lairage without AMI. This is not in line with Article 45(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

audits.title: Hygiene, traceability and channelling of animal by-products (ABP) and derived products (DP)

recommendations.text: To ensure that the list of establishments, plants and operators handling ABP and DP is kept updated, in line with Article 47(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: Whilst the SVFA has developed a website with the lists of registered and approved ABP establishments which was in line the technical specifications for the format of such lists (available on the web page: https://ec.europa.eu/food/sites/food/files/safety/docs/fs- animal-products-app-est-technical_spec_04032012_en.pdf), the audit team noted that the details of some of the ABP establishments were not up-to-date, contrary to the requirements of Article 47(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and Article 20a of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. For example: Some ABP establishments appeared on the list with the remark `temporary approval' until a date in 2018, although such an approval can be granted only for a maximum period of six months, The storage plant visited is included in the list of approved plants carrying out intermediate activities and plants/establishments storing ABP (Section I of the above technical specifications) for storage of Category 1 and 2 materials, and is listed with the prefix "COLC" reserved for collection centres in the technical specifications. The use of the prefix is not correct as the activities of the storage plant visited do not fall under the definition of a collection centre as specified in point 53 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, One of the operators visited was still registered for transporting Category 1 and 2 ABP but stated that his company had ceased this activity two years ago, and The national legislation allows granting derogations to use some ABP for specific feeding purposes for a 3­year period only. The SVFA grants such derogations for feeding of zoo animals, circus animals, reptiles and birds of prey other than zoo and circus animals, fur animals, wild animals, dogs in recognised dog kennels, or pack of hounds. Contrary to the national provisions, some operators appeared still on the list of these registered ABP operators with derogations, although the derogations had expired in 2018 or 2019. Conclusions on the registration, approval and listing of ABP plants, establishments and operators

Inaccurate statuses recorded in the lists of approved ABP operators, plants and establishments indicate that despite changes in the activities of individual operators the information contained in the lists remain unchanged. Delayed or absent notification of changes related to operators' activities result in lists not being up-to- date and as a consequence can affect the planning of official controls and result in official controls being scheduled for operators which are no longer active and exclude operators which has only recently received their registration/approval.

recommendations.text: To ensure that prior to issuing an approval for a processing plant, as provided for in Article 44(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the competent authority checks that a validation of the plant has been carried out by the operator, as required by Section 2 of Chapter I of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: The SVFA has established a procedure for approval of ABP plants which meets the requirements of Article 44 of Regulation (EU) No 1069/2009. Despite applying the procedure during the approval process, in two out of five ABP plants visited the available approval-related documentation did not demonstrate that the competent authority had checked if the plant operators had carried out validation of processing in accordance with all of the procedures and indicators required by Section 2 of Chapter 1 of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. For example: An ABP plant processing Category 3 material had received an approval even though the operator's documentation did not clearly demonstrate that the validation of the processing method used (method 7) met all of the specific process requirements laid down in point G of Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011(2). The operator's records presented during the audit indicated that the operator had validated a processing method which was relevant for the production of a product for human consumption ­ an earlier step of the processing chain, from which some remaining material was used for the production of PAP and fat - rather than a processing method relevant for the production of DP (PAP and fats); In another ABP processing plant using Category 3 material, the competent authority granted the approval even though the validation file for the processing method 7 was incomplete. The heating process identified as a CCP, required heating of the raw material to a minimum core temperature of 100°C for 60 minutes. The validation charts did not indicate the time when the process started and ended, thus did not allow to assess when and where to measure the exposure time for the required temperature parameter. The audit team noted that neither of the above mentioned operators had reported issues regarding the microbiological quality of the final product and that the results of the (2) In its response to the draft report the competent authority noted that supporting documentation relating to the official inspection for approval purposes is held by the SVFA and not the DVFA. 7 microbiological tests performed by both the operator and the competent authority were compliant.

Most of the inspectors interviewed by the audit team were not aware about the sampling requirements for validation of the processing method 7 provided for in point G of Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 142/2011 and thus were unable to carry out the checks required by Section 2 of Chapter 1 of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 prior to granting the approval.

While adequate procedures exist for registration and approval of ABP operators, plants and establishments, inaccuracies in their implementation, identified in processing plants in relation to the assessment of the processing method 7 validation, 8 weaken their effectiveness.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the operators' past records as regards the outcome of official controls performed on them and their compliance with the rules for ABP and DP are taken into account when establishing official control frequencies, as required by Article 9(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The SVFA decides on the inspection frequencies based on risk factors such as the intended use of the commodity (e.g. feed or for technical use), seasonality (or not) of production and size of the establishment. The inspectors at district level can increase the inspection frequency if they consider it justified based on their local risk assessment. The methodological instructions contain guidance on the risk factors to be taken into account for this purpose. Contrary to Article 9(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, the 9 compliance history of the establishment is not included in the risk factors. The audit team noted that in none of the establishments visited had the shortcomings detected during the previous inspection led to an increase in the inspection frequency. The SVFA representative stated that the DVFA staff rarely increase the inspection frequency.

While the inspection frequencies are established without taking into account the past performance of the operator, this deficiency is largely mitigated by the effective follow-up actions, including additional inspections and sampling where relevant, taken when cases of non-compliance are identified during routine inspections.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the official controls in processing plants, carried out in accordance with Article 32(3)(a) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 and Section 1 of Chapter 1 of Annex XVI to the said Regulation, are effective and appropriate, as provided for in Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Regarding the general hygiene checks, the installations and equipment seen in the plants visited were in adequate condition and the general hygiene requirements were complied with, with the exception of an ABP plant processing Category 3 material where the audit team noted certain shortcomings that had not been recorded in earlier inspection reports. In particular, some of the plastic containers used were very dirty and broken and the clean area was insufficiently protected against rodents and pests (the doors were not properly fitted and as a consequence there were gaps allowing entering of insects and mice), contrary to Article 25(1)(c) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

Concerning the official controls on the effective implementation of the permanent written procedure based on the HACCP principles, including operator's own checks and the standards of the products after processing, the audit team noted that all plants 11 visited established such procedures and carried out own controls and these were checked by the inspectors.

The audit team examined several inspection reports and noted that these had not identified a number of shortcomings in relation to the permanent written procedure based on the HACCP principles in the two plants processing Category 3 material visited. The procedures were not in line with the requirements of Article 29 of Regulation (EU) No 1069/2009 regarding the following points: In line with point 1(a) of Section 4 of Chapter II of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, in one of the processing plants, the size of the raw material particles before feeding into the cooker was identified as a CCP. However, the CCP was checked by the operator (`monitored') only once a year. This is contrary to Article 29(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) No 1069/2009 which requires to establish and implement effective monitoring at CCPs. Evidence of annual calibration of measuring devices was available. However, in the other processing plant visited, the range of calibration of the thermometers covered only the range of the CCP point limit upwards which does not ensure correct monitoring of the processing conditions required by point 1 of Section 2 of Chapter II of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

The sampling and testing regimes and the procedure followed for ABP sampling of the final products as part of the operators' own checks were largely satisfactory in the plants visited. The laboratory results of the examinations assessed by the audit team were also satisfactory. However, the audit team noted that the procedures for microbiological sampling as part of own checks were not compliant with the requirements of Chapter I of Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 and this was not noted during previous official controls: Only one sample of the end product destined as feed material for analysis of Salmonella was taken instead of the five required. In one of the Category 3 ABP processing plants, some of the own check samples for Salmonella were taken from the product at 90°C (at which temperature Salmonella will not survive) instead of taking it in the final product in the storage area or before dispatch.

In one of the plants processing Category 3 material, the PAP destined for production of petfood contained small but clearly visible plastic particles originating from plastic 12 wrapping or otherwise packaging materials. The audit team noted that the operator had in place a sieve which allowed for capturing particles of a bigger size. The presence of packaging materials in feedstuffs is contrary to the requirements of Article 6 and Point 7 of Chapter I of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council and was not detected by the inspectors during previous controls.

Concerning the checks on storage conditions, the audit team noted that in one of the plants processing Category 3 material, the raw ABP comprising raw meat and fats from slaughterhouses (including ABP from other Member States) destined for production of processed petfood was stored in rooms without temperature control. The operator stated that the raw material would be processed within 24 hours and considered that no cooling was necessary. However, the fact that the ABP was undergoing fermentation suggests that the products were stored at ambient temperature for longer than 24 hours from their delivery to the plant. The lack of suitable temperature-controlled storage facilities for incoming material was not noted during previous official inspections. This is contrary to point 1(f) of Section 1, and point 3 of Section 2, of Chapter II of Annex IX to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. 5.3.3.2 Official controls in other ABP establishments

Although relatively frequent, the official controls on certain topics are superficial and ineffective in identifying non-compliances in relation to the general hygiene requirements, the permanent written procedures based on the HACCP principles, some areas of own checks and traceability and record keeping.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the official controls on operators handling ABP and DP, carried out in accordance with Article 32(3)(b) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 and Sections 1 to 9 of Chapter III of Annex XVI to the said Regulation, are effective and appropriate, as provided for in Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In the DVFAs visited, the official controls on ABP covered identification of ABP. Nonetheless, the audit team noted the following shortcomings in relation to identification of ABP: In the OF/SI plant, the operator kept some big bags and plastic containers not bearing any identification descriptions and filled with raw ABP and some other products; the plant representative explained that these were raw material and final products for and from production of OF/SI, and In the multispecies slaughterhouse with a cutting plant, some ABP had been collected in containers which did not bear identification of the category and the required warning sentence. 13 All the above is not in line with Point 2 of Chapter II of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, requiring proper identification of stored ABP.

Regarding traceability, evidence was available that during inspections the competent authorities check the availability of documentation that is required in the national and EU legislation (for example, in slaughterhouses; ante and post-mortem inspection logbooks, information on quantities of SRM removed and ABP generated, commercial documents and health certificates, if applicable). However, the audit team noted that the official controls in some of the establishments visited have not included the checks on records or, when they covered the record keeping, did not detect a number of non- compliances with Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and the relevant requirements of Chapter III and Chapter IV of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

The records of previous inspections in the OF/SI plant visited did not contain any remarks on record keeping, even though in line with Section 7 of Chapter III of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, official controls of OF/SI plants must always include a check on the records kept by the operator. The audit team noted that the operator does not keep any register of incoming and outgoing materials or commercial documents for consignments of raw ABP received from another Member State, contrary to the requirements of Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and point 2 of Chapter III of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. These non-compliances were not noted during previous inspections.

In the ABP storage plant visited, a register of incoming ABP was available. However, the number of copies of commercial documents issued at the place of ABP origin kept in the register was lower than the number of ABP consignments handled by the storage plant. The inspector responsible for the controls explained that, in most cases, commercial documents were forwarded directly to the head office of the storage plant. The inspector did not however verify if the commercial documents are indeed available at the head office, contrary to Article 32(2) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, which requires that official controls must include checks on the keeping of records, including other documents.

The audit team examined several inspection reports and noted that these had not identified a number of shortcomings in relation to the permanent written procedure based on the HACCP principles. These were not fully in line with the requirements of Article 29 of Regulation (EU) No 1069/2009 regarding the following points: In the Category 1 and 2 storage plant visited, the procedures seen belonged to the mother company and were not adjusted for this site. There was no documented evidence of carrying out some of the own checks described in the procedures (e.g. pest control), 14 In the plant producing OF/SI, the procedures had not been updated and there were shortcomings in their implementation as there were no records of CCP monitoring. The HACCP team had not been nominated and no HACCP review had been carried out.

Concerning the general hygiene, the audit team noted in the storage plant visited that in the previous last inspection report the competent authority had only recorded one shortcoming whereas during the on-the-spot visit the audit team noted several others which concerned the collection of the ABP and the maintenance and cleaning of the site and equipment: The containers on-the-spot for collection and transport of ABP had no lids or other kinds of cover and were dirty with deposits of rotten materials from previous loads. A register was available for cleaning of trucks. However, there was no instruction for the drivers on how to clean and if needed, disinfect the containers. The official veterinarian responsible for the controls stated that he had instructed the drivers to use the disinfection product undiluted; the audit team noted that this was against the instruction on the disinfectant label. The above is not in line with the requirements laid down in Section 1 of Chapter I of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. In addition, the waste water trap was filthy and blocked up and not allowing for effective drainage of the waste water, contrary to Article 25(1)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

Although relatively frequent, the official controls on certain topics are superficial and ineffective in identifying non-compliances in relation to the general hygiene requirements, the permanent written procedures based on the HACCP principles, some areas of own checks and traceability and record keeping.

citations.text: For the testosterone (in serum) case the competent authority failed to ensure compliance with EU requirements (17). In this case the audit team noted considerable delays in conducting follow-up activities. The investigation was initiated with an on-the spot visit eight months after the non-compliant result was detected and following several requests for information from the central level. The suspect samples, taken during the on-the-spot visit, were rejected by the laboratory as they had deteriorated and the sampling was not repeated. One year after the identification of the non-compliant result, and without any further action to complete the investigation, all of the animals from the affected farm were moved out of the farm (with the authorisation of the DVFA) and traded to another Member State.

The SVFA explained that human resource-related constraints were the origin of the significant shortfalls noted in this case. Changes had been recently introduced in the respective DVFA team and that additional sampling at this farm is planned for 2021. However, no action has been taken to update the documented procedures in order to ensure that, should a similar situation reoccur in future, adequate corrective actions and coordination measures would be put in place in a timely manner to guarantee the effectiveness of the official controls, i.e. proper investigation of the non-compliant results, as required under the EU legislation (18). Conclusions on follow-up of non-compliant results

The planned arrangements for investigating non-compliant residues results are well established and could provide for an effective investigation of non-compliant results. However, deficiencies were noted in the competent authority's ability to ensure its consistent implementation.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently check that feed business operators meet the requirements for hazard identification in their respective hazard analysis and critical control point plans, and that the result is recorded in the report of said controls.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In all of the five establishments visited, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. The audit team noted that the inspectors' assessment of the hazard identification part of the HACCP plan was deficient in four establishments. In general, the hazard identification section of the operators' HACCP plans was incorrect (certain relevant hazards were not mentioned such as pesticides, mycotoxins, dioxins, although these were relevant for different feed materials or heavy metals relevant for additives/premixtures) or very generic without the level of detail necessary for a proper hazard identification (as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005) and consequent risk assessment. This issue was not reflected in the inspection reports seen by the auditors and operators were thus unaware that there was a deficiency. The audit team noted that, when interviewed during the audit, some inspectors correctly identified these deficiencies.

In one feed material producer the company used direct drying during its production process. In the hazard analyses this processing step was not assessed at all. The company did not include dioxin tests in its own sampling plan. This potential risk was overlooked during previous official controls.

While the planning of inspections is largely based on appropriate risk-related factors and allows for official controls to be carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency, the effectiveness of controls is weakened by shortcomings in inspectors' assessment of (i) feed business operators' hazard identifications within their HACCP systems, (ii) operators' tests on cross-contamination, and (iii) operators' compliance with labelling requirements. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis Planning of official sampling

audits.title: Emergency preparedness in the plant health sector

recommendations.text: Ensure that each contingency plan contains sufficient detail regarding Competent Authorities access to equipment, personnel, external expertise, and resources necessary for the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, containment of the priority pest concerned as required by Article 25(2)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

citations.text: The audit team examined the contingency plans for X. fastidiosa, B. xylophilus and A. planipennis. In general, the selected contingency plans contain the information required by Article 25(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, however the plans lack some relevant details. Specifically, the plans lack sufficient detail on CA's access to specific resources when required such as access to machinery needed for felling of trees, access to extra personnel required to undertake additional surveys when demarcated areas are established and any other services needed under extraordinary circumstances for the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, containment of the priority pest concerned as required by Article 25(2)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

Slovakia has developed procedures to eradicate outbreaks of priority pests with contingency plans prepared and simulation exercises being undertaken. However, the published contingency plans do not include all the necessary detail to help the authorities rapidly and effectively eradicate any established priority pests, which may delay the implementation of eradication measures and containment of the outbreaks.

audits.title: evaluate the system of official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union and verification of compliance of border control posts with European Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authority at the border control post of introduction in Slovakia takes appropriate follow-up measures when it does not receive confirmation of arrival from the place of destination for consignments of goods of animal origin authorised for transit.

citations.text: The audit team noted that, according to the CHEDs evaluated and data in TRACES-NT for the period January 2023 to November 2024, only eight of 31 consignments of goods of animal origin authorised for direct transit at a BCP of introduction in Slovakia had their arrival at the exit BCP in another Member State confirmed in Part III of the CHED. The SVFA stated that it does not follow-up on these consignments, which is not in line with Article 20 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2124 and its own documented procedures. 9 5.2.4 Documentary, identity and physical checks of consignments 5.2.4.1 Checks on consignments of animals

However, some shortcomings were noted in the performance of official controls on 12 goods of animal origin and the decision-making and follow-up of consignments of goods of non-animal origin transferred to control points. The competent authorities took corrective actions to address the majority of these shortcomings, thereby minimising the risk of non-compliant animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Slovakia.
